title: Food and Nutrition
description: Ten calm, informative pieces about food and the body: how we use protein, fats and carbohydrates, reading a label, the Mediterranean diet, a school cafeteria, the history of vitamins, fiber and the gut, food deserts, a dietitian's myths column, a school play about vegetables and a Scottish harvest festival.

lessons.title: What a High Jumper Eats
lessons.summary: A college high jumper learns from a sports nutrition expert how her body uses protein, carbohydrates and fats.
lessons.text:
Lena Ortiz is a high jumper on her college track team, and for most of her first year she ate like many busy students: a heap of pasta at night, coffee in the morning and a few snacks in between. By spring, she felt tired before practice had even begun. Her coach suggested that she talk to the team's nutrition expert, a calm woman named Grace Kim.

"Food does three main jobs," Grace said. "It gives you energy, it gives you building material, and it keeps the machinery running. Protein, fats and carbohydrates each play their part, and a jumper needs all three."

She started with protein. Every time Lena trained, Grace explained, tiny tears formed in her muscles, especially in the calf, the muscle at the back of the lower leg that pushes her off the ground. To repair those tears, the body breaks the protein in food into smaller pieces and uses them to build new muscle, a process called protein synthesis. Synthesis simply means putting parts together to make something new. Eating some protein at every meal, rather than all of it at dinner, keeps that synthesis going through the day. Protein also helps the immune system defend the body against an attacker such as a virus, so a steady supply prepares the body for each attacker.

Next came carbohydrates, the body's favorite fuel for fast, powerful movement. Sweet snacks, Grace said, burn like paper: a bright flash, then nothing. Whole grains, beans and fruit burn more like wood, and they help stabilize the amount of sugar in the blood, so that energy stays steady. "If you want to stabilize your energy for practice," she said, "eat a real meal two or three hours before, not a candy bar ten minutes before."

Finally, she talked about fats, which many of Lena's teammates feared. Fats store energy, help the body absorb certain vitamins and form part of the thin wall around every cell. They also protect the nerves, which carry tiny electrical signals called impulses. Every jump begins with an impulse that travels from the brain down to the legs. Lena mentioned that her calf sometimes gave a little twitch after hard sessions. Grace said that a small twitch is usually just a sign of a tired muscle.

Over the next months, Lena made small changes. She did not shorten her training; instead, she learned to shorten the gap between practice and her next real meal. She still enjoyed a heap of pasta, but now it came with chicken and vegetables. Her energy, once so fragile that one missed meal could ruin a day, became steady. She no longer felt fragile at the end of a long week.

At the end of the season, Lena jumped higher than ever before. Food was not magic, she knew, but it had become part of her training.

Questions:
Why did Lena go to see Grace?
She felt tired before practice, and her coach suggested that she talk to Grace.
What is protein synthesis?
It is the process in which the body uses pieces of protein from food to build new muscle.
How did Grace compare different kinds of carbohydrates?
She said that sweet snacks burn like paper, while whole grains, beans and fruit burn more like wood.
What do fats do for the nerves?
They protect the nerves, which carry the impulses that start every jump.
What changes did Lena make?
She ate sooner after practice and added chicken and vegetables to her pasta.

lessons.title: Reading a Food Label
lessons.summary: A short guide walks through the Nutrition Facts label of an imaginary breakfast bar, line by line.
lessons.text:
Pick up almost any package of food in a grocery store in the United States, turn it over, and you will find the same black and white box. It is called the Nutrition Facts label, and it follows a template set by the government: the same rows, in the same order, in the same plain type. Because every company must use this template, you can compare two very different products in a few seconds, once you know where to look.

To see how it works, imagine a breakfast bar called Sunny Oat. The product is fictional, but its numbers are typical, and a fictional example lets us look closely without blaming any real company.

At the top of the label is the serving size: one bar. This is the most important line, and the one that people most often skip. Every number below it describes one serving, so if you eat two bars, you must double everything.

Next comes the number of calories, followed by fat, sodium, carbohydrates, fiber, sugars and protein. The accompanying percentage, called the Daily Value, tells you how much of a day's typical amount one serving provides. The percentages assume a diet of 2,000 calories a day. That figure is somewhat arbitrary, a round number chosen for convenience, and many people need more or less. Even so, an arbitrary measure can still be useful, as long as you read it as a rough guide. A simple rule helps: 5 percent or less is low, and 20 percent or more is high.

Below the box, you will find the accompanying list of ingredients. The law requires that ingredients appear in order of weight, from the most to the least. If sugar appears near the start, the bar contains a lot of it. A lengthy list is not always a bad sign, since a bar full of nuts and dried fruit may have many ingredients. Still, a lengthy list of unfamiliar chemical names is worth a second look.

The front of the package is a different matter. That is where companies place the words they consider most desirable, such as "natural" or "made with whole grains." Some of these phrases mean very little. A specific health claim, however, such as a statement that a food may lower the risk of heart disease, needs authorization from regulators, and that authorization depends on scientific evidence. When companies and regulators disagree about what a word may mean, the question sometimes ends up before the judiciary, and judges, rather than scientists, have the final say. In this way, the judiciary has also helped to shape the words on labels.

You need not study every package. Reading labels works best as a deliberate habit for the foods you buy often. Make a deliberate choice once, at home or in the store, and you will not need to think about it again each week. The desirable result is not perfection, just a clearer idea of what is on your plate.

Questions:
Why is the label's template useful?
Because every company uses the same template, people can compare products quickly.
Why does the guide use a fictional bar?
A fictional example lets readers look closely without blaming a real company.
What do the Daily Value percentages assume?
They assume a diet of 2,000 calories a day, which is a somewhat arbitrary figure.
How are the ingredients listed?
They are listed in order of weight, from the most to the least.
What does a specific health claim need?
It needs authorization from regulators, based on scientific evidence.

lessons.title: The Mediterranean Diet, Weighed Calmly
lessons.summary: A columnist looks at what the research on the Mediterranean diet shows, where its limits are, and what is worth keeping.
lessons.text:
Few ways of eating have been praised as highly as the Mediterranean diet. The pictures are familiar: a table on a balcony above a small marina, a bowl of tomatoes, a bottle of olive oil, the perfume of lemon trees in the warm air, and a couple in their eighties laughing over a long lunch. Much of this picture rests on good science, but it is worth weighing the evidence with a cool head.

The idea took shape in the middle of the last century, when researchers noticed that people in parts of Greece and southern Italy seemed to have fewer heart problems than people in the United States. Their meals were built around vegetables, beans, whole grains, fruit, nuts and olive oil, with fish a few times a week, little red meat and few sweets. Many of them stayed active well into their eighties, climbing steep streets and working in their gardens.

Since then, large studies have followed thousands of people for years. Each respondent answers questions about what he or she eats, and researchers compare the answers with health over time. In general, people who adhere closely to this pattern tend to have lower rates of heart disease than those who do not. In one well-known trial, participants who were asked to adhere to a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil or nuts did somewhat better than a group given general advice to eat less fat.

There are, however, honest limits. Surveys depend on memory, and a respondent does not always remember what he or she ate last month. People who eat this way may also smoke less, sleep more or have closer families, and it is hard to separate the food from the life around it. Critics also warn against advice from an ivory tower. Experts in an ivory tower may forget that fresh fish and good olive oil can be expensive, and that not every family lives near a marina where boats bring in the morning catch.

The good news is that the heart of the diet costs very little. Beans, onions, frozen vegetables and canned fish are cheap. You do not need a balcony with a view of the sea; a kitchen table works just as well. What matters most is the overall pattern, not any single food.

Perhaps the most valuable part of the tradition is also the most endangered. In many villages, long meals shared with family are giving way to fast food and busy schedules, and some visitors say that the traditional diet is now endangered in the very places that made it famous. For many families there, the shared meal was symbolic, a sign that the day had a center. That symbolic value, along with the perfume of garlic and herbs from a busy kitchen, may be worth keeping, wherever we live.

Questions:
What did researchers notice in the middle of the last century?
They noticed that people in parts of Greece and southern Italy seemed to have fewer heart problems than people in the United States.
What do large studies suggest about people who adhere to this pattern?
They tend to have lower rates of heart disease than those who do not.
Why are surveys an honest limit?
They depend on memory, and a respondent does not always remember what he or she ate.
What part of the diet costs very little?
Beans, onions, frozen vegetables and canned fish are cheap.
Why was the shared meal symbolic?
It was a sign that the day had a center.

lessons.title: The New Lunch Menu
lessons.summary: A school kitchen manager tries to make lunch healthier, fails at first, and succeeds by listening to students and their families.
lessons.text:
When Rosa Delgado became the kitchen manager at Lincoln High School, the lunch menu had not changed in ten years. Pizza, fries and a burger combo were served every day, and the burger combo was by far the most popular choice. Wanting something healthier, Rosa replaced the fries with plain brown rice and added a large green salad to every tray.

The change was a flop. Students threw the salad away and left the brown rice on their trays. Within two weeks, sales had fallen so far that the principal asked whether the new menu should stay. Rosa admitted that it was a flop. "I tried to change what adolescents eat without asking a single adolescent," she said later. "That was my mistake."

That winter, she read about behavioral research on school lunches. Behavioral scientists had found that small changes in how food is offered can matter more than lectures. Fruit placed near the register sells better than fruit hidden at the back. A dish with an appealing name sells better than one called "vegetable side." Rosa moved the fruit, gave her dishes better names and created a new combo: a main dish, a piece of fruit and milk, for the same price as the old burger combo.

Next, she asked the students what they ate at home. Lincoln High was a school of many nationalities, and a single class might include students of five nationalities, each with its own family dishes. One girl, Ana, told Rosa about her grandmother's mole, a rich, dark sauce from Mexico made with chili peppers, spices and a little chocolate. Ana's grandmother came to the school kitchen and taught the staff to make chicken in mole. Other families sent recipes for rice and beans, chicken curry and vegetable soup. Rosa kept them all in a thick blue folder, and by spring the folder held more than forty recipes.

The school bulletin, a weekly page sent to parents, began to announce each new dish and the family who had shared it. Parents wrote in to suggest more, and the bulletin soon had a regular section called "Recipe of the Week."

Not every change was welcome. When the soda machines were removed from the main hall, a student wrote in the school newspaper that the decision was a form of censorship. The principal replied that it was not censorship: students could still bring whatever they liked from home, and the school had simply chosen what it would sell. Rosa understood the student's feelings. Teenagers value their autonomy, and they dislike being told what to do. So she added a salad bar where students could build their own plates, which gave them autonomy without fries at every meal.

By the end of the year, sales were higher than ever. The chicken in mole had become the most popular dish of all, and Ana's grandmother was invited back to teach two more recipes.

Questions:
Why was the first new menu a flop?
Rosa tried to change what adolescents ate without asking them, and students threw the food away.
What did behavioral research teach Rosa?
It taught her that small changes in how food is offered can matter more than lectures.
What is mole?
It is a rich, dark sauce from Mexico made with chili peppers, spices and a little chocolate.
What did the school bulletin do?
It announced each new dish and the family who had shared it.
How did the salad bar help?
It gave students autonomy, because they could build their own plates.

lessons.title: Something Missing: A Short History of Vitamins
lessons.summary: How scientists slowly learned that some diseases are caused not by germs but by the lack of tiny substances in food.
lessons.text:
For most of history, people believed that illness came from something added to the body: bad air, poison or, later, germs. The idea that a disease could come from something missing took a long time to accept. That realization, when it finally came, changed the way we think about food.

The first clues came from the sea. On long voyages, sailors often developed scurvy: their gums bled, their wounds would not heal, and many died. In 1747, a ship's doctor named James Lind gave different foods to groups of sick sailors and found that those who ate oranges and lemons recovered quickly. Lind did not know why the fruit worked.

More than a century later, a doctor named Christiaan Eijkman was studying a nerve disease among soldiers in Asia. He noticed that chickens fed on polished white rice developed similar problems, while chickens fed on brown rice stayed healthy. Something in the outer layer of the grain, removed by polishing, seemed to protect them. In 1912, the scientist Casimir Funk suggested that several diseases were caused by the lack of such substances, and he gave them a name that became "vitamins." The realization that food contains such vital substances spread quickly. In 1922, two researchers in California found that rats needed an unknown factor in their food for normal reproduction. Without it, reproduction failed; with it, the rats had healthy young. The factor became known as vitamin E.

Light mattered too. In industrial cities, many children grew up with weak, bent legs. Doctors noticed that these children got little daylight, especially in winter, when daylight was short and the air was dark with smoke. Cod liver oil helped, and so did sunlight. Scientists later learned that the skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to sunlight. Light was also used against tuberculosis. In 1903, the Danish doctor Niels Finsen received the prestigious Nobel Prize for treating a form of tuberculosis of the skin with strong light. Later, Eijkman, too, received this prestigious prize for his work with rice.

Not every lesson was about having too little. Polar explorers discovered that the liver of a polar bear contains so much vitamin A that a large meal of it can be lethal. Vitamins, it turned out, follow the old rule that the dose makes the poison: an amount that helps can become lethal when it is many times larger.

This history still matters. In many countries, a newborn baby receives a small dose of vitamin K soon after birth, because a newborn has very little of it, and vitamin K helps the blood work properly. Doctors can measure vitamin levels in serum, the clear liquid part of the blood, and a serum test often guides their advice. Vitamins are also sold everywhere as capsules, but most experts agree that a capsule is no replacement for a varied diet, which provides vitamins along with everything else food has to offer.

Questions:
What did James Lind find in 1747?
He found that sick sailors who ate oranges and lemons recovered quickly.
What did Eijkman notice about chickens?
Chickens fed on polished white rice became sick, while those fed on brown rice stayed healthy.
What did the researchers in California discover in 1922?
They found that rats needed an unknown factor, later called vitamin E, for normal reproduction.
How was light used against tuberculosis?
Niels Finsen treated a form of tuberculosis of the skin with strong light.
Why does a newborn baby often receive vitamin K?
A newborn has very little vitamin K, which helps the blood work properly.

lessons.title: A Month of Fiber
lessons.summary: An office worker spends a month adding fiber to his meals and learns how it feeds the bacteria in his gut.
lessons.text:
My name is Ben, and until last spring I knew almost nothing about fiber. I worked long days at a desk and spent most evenings on the sofa in front of the television. Then, one evening on that sofa, I read an article which said that most adults in the United States eat only about half the fiber that experts recommend. I decided to spend one month changing that.

I bought a small notebook and wrote down everything I ate. My breakfast was white toast, my lunch was a sandwich on white bread, and my dinner was often pasta. There were very few beans, whole grains, vegetables or fruits, which are the main sources of fiber.

I also read about what fiber does. It is the part of plant food that our bodies cannot break down on their own. It passes through the stomach and reaches the lower part of the gut, where trillions of bacteria live. To these bacteria, fiber is dinner. As they feed on it, they produce substances that help keep the gut wall healthy and strong. Some of the bacteria cling to a thin protective layer that covers the wall, and fiber helps them cling there, rather than leaving room for less friendly kinds. I also learned that the gut has its own network of nerves, so large that it can work in an almost autonomous way, without waiting for orders from the brain. Some scientists call it the "second brain," and its autonomous work never stops.

I did not want to be saddled with a complicated plan, so I chose three simple rules: whole grain bread instead of white, one serving of beans or peas every day, and fruit instead of cookies after lunch. Canned beans were easy, but dried beans were cheaper, and they needed to soak overnight before cooking. On Sunday nights, I would soak a large pot of them, cook them on Monday, and eat them all week.

The first week was not comfortable. I felt full of gas, and my stomach made noises during meetings. I read that this is common, and that the gut bacteria need time to adjust. People who increase fiber are usually advised to do it gradually and to drink plenty of water, so that they are not saddled with problems that make them give up. I slowed down a little, and by the second week, the problem had passed.

By the end of the month, my notebook looked very different. I was eating beans, whole grains and fruit every day, and I felt steadier between meals. I still spend some evenings on the sofa, but now with a bowl of berries rather than a bag of chips. Fiber, I learned, does not work overnight, but it does repay patience. It will repay the effort of a slow start many times over.

Questions:
Why did Ben decide to spend a month eating more fiber?
He read that most adults in the United States eat only about half the fiber that experts recommend.
What did his notebook show at the start?
It showed that he ate very few beans, whole grains, vegetables or fruits.
What do gut bacteria do with fiber?
They feed on it and produce substances that help keep the gut wall healthy.
Why is the gut sometimes called the second brain?
It has its own network of nerves that can work in an almost autonomous way.
What did Ben do with dried beans?
He would soak them overnight on Sunday and cook them on Monday.

lessons.title: Living in a Food Desert
lessons.summary: A report on one city neighborhood without a supermarket, and on what its residents did to bring fresh food closer.
lessons.text:
In the United States, researchers use the term "food desert" for an area where many people have low incomes and the nearest supermarket is far away, usually more than a mile in a city. Much of the food there is sold in small corner stores, where chips and soda are easy to find and fresh vegetables are not. Elm Park, on the east side of a large city, is a typical example.

Elm Park once had two supermarkets. Over the years, both companies decided to relocate to the suburbs, where land was cheaper and customers had cars. Then the city announced the cancellation of the bus route that ran to the nearest supermarket. For older residents without cars, the cancellation turned a short trip into a journey of more than an hour.

Residents also noticed a large price differential between the corner stores and the suburban supermarkets: the same bag of apples could cost almost twice as much in Elm Park. Store owners explained that the differential was not only about profit. The logistics of fresh food are difficult for a small shop. Fruit and vegetables spoil quickly, trucks deliver in large amounts, and a small store cannot sell enough to keep prices low. The logistics favor big stores, and big stores had left.

When covid arrived, things grew harder. Many residents feared crowded buses, and online delivery rarely reached their streets. During the worst months of covid, a church and a food bank handed out food parcels every Saturday. Each parcel held rice, canned beans, milk and, when possible, fresh fruit. The parcels helped, but they were not a long-term answer.

The longer answer began on a parcel of empty land behind the old library. A group of residents decided to stop waiting. They built raised beds and grew tomatoes, greens and peppers. Instead of chemicals, they relied on helpful insects, such as the assassin bug, a small hunter that eats other insects that damage vegetables. The children loved the name and searched the leaves for an assassin bug every week.

News of the garden spread in an unexpected place: the local barber shop. Marcus Hill, a barber who had cut hair in Elm Park for thirty years, began talking about the garden with every customer. Once a month, he also invited a nurse who checked blood pressure and talked about salt. "People trust their barber," Marcus said. "So I try to deserve it."

The group now speaks of food sovereignty, the idea that a community should have real control over how its food is grown and sold. For them, sovereignty does not mean refusing help; it means having a voice. Their goal is to empower residents, not to rescue them. A small market owned by the neighborhood is planned for next year, and its founders hope it will empower the next generation too.

Questions:
What is a food desert?
It is an area where many people have low incomes and the nearest supermarket is far away.
Why did the cancellation of the bus route matter?
Older residents without cars now needed more than an hour to reach a supermarket.
Why are the logistics of fresh food hard for small stores?
Fresh food spoils quickly, trucks deliver in large amounts, and small stores cannot sell enough.
Why did the supermarkets relocate?
They chose to relocate to the suburbs, where land was cheaper and customers had cars.
What does food sovereignty mean to the group?
It means that the community should have real control over its food.

lessons.title: Five Myths from My Mailbox
lessons.summary: A dietitian answers readers' letters about microwaves, vitamin C, chocolate, "good" and "bad" foods, and eating in hard times.
lessons.text:
As a dietitian, I get questions from readers every week, and many begin with something they heard from a friend or read online. My modus operandi, or way of working, never changes: I find the best studies, read them carefully and tell you what they show. A modus operandi is only useful if you stick to it. As always, a short bibliography for this column appears on our website, so that you can check my sources.

Myth one: microwave ovens make food radioactive. They do not. A microwave oven makes the water in food move faster, and that movement produces heat. Radioactive materials such as uranium give off a very different kind of energy, and there is no uranium, or anything like it, inside your microwave. Your soup is simply warm.

Myth two: large doses of vitamin C will cure a cold. When researchers compare vitamin C with a placebo, a pill that contains nothing active, they find little difference for most people once a cold has begun. Many people do feel better after taking a pill, but much of that comes from the placebo effect, the comfort of expecting relief.

Myth three: chocolate is health food. A reader who received a box of dark chocolates as a valentine asks whether it counts as health food. Dark chocolate contains useful plant substances, but also plenty of sugar and fat. Enjoy your valentine slowly, with pleasure, and do not think of it as medicine.

Myth four: some foods are good, some foods are bad, and so are the people who eat them. Food has no morality. A cookie is not a sin, and a salad is not a virtue. When friends brag about skipping dinner or cutting out bread, they are turning eating into a test of character. You do not need to brag, or to listen to others brag, to eat well. Writers in the tradition of feminism have long pointed out that talk about food and morality falls especially hard on women, who are often judged by what is on their plates. Several books on feminism and food appear in this month's bibliography.

Myth five: eating for comfort is always a failure. A reader whose father died this spring wrote that she felt guilty for living on soup and toast for weeks. I want to tell her gently that food has always been part of how people carry sorrow. In a time of sorrow, a warm bowl of soup is not a weakness; it is care.

Finally, a word about a belief I meet more often than any myth: "I will never be able to eat well." Such a sentence can turn into a self-fulfilling prophecy. If we expect to fail, we stop trying. You can break that prophecy with one small change, made this week, and another the next.

Questions:
What is the writer's modus operandi?
The writer finds the best studies, reads them carefully and reports what they show.
Can a microwave oven make food radioactive?
No, it cannot, and there is no uranium or anything like it inside a microwave.
What do studies show when vitamin C is compared with a placebo?
They show little difference for most people once a cold has begun.
What does the writer say about food and morality?
The writer says that food has no morality: a cookie is not a sin, and a salad is not a virtue.
How can a reader break a self-fulfilling prophecy?
The reader can make one small change this week and another the next.

lessons.title: The Vegetable Avengers
lessons.summary: A teacher writes a school play about vegetables, and her second grade class performs it for their families.
lessons.text:
Every year, Ms. Abara's second grade class put on a short play during the school's Healthy Eating Week. That fall, she wanted the play to be about vegetables. She had noticed that many parents tried to bribe their children with dessert: "Two more bites of peas, and you can have ice cream." Ms. Abara understood why parents did it, but she had read that when adults bribe children to eat a food, the children often decide that the food must be unpleasant. She hoped a play could make vegetables exciting.

She called the play "The Vegetable Avengers." Each child would play an avenger, a hero who protects the town. There was Captain Pea, who was small but brave; Tomato Girl, who was quick and bright; and Pumpkin Boy, who was slow but very strong. The storyline was simple. A dragon made of candy arrives in town and takes away everyone's energy, so that nobody wants to run or play. The avengers set out to stop him.

In her first draft, the heroes slay the dragon with swords made of green beans. When she read it to the class, however, several children did not want the heroes to slay anyone. "Maybe the dragon is just hungry," one boy said. Ms. Abara liked the idea, so she changed the storyline. In the new version, the avengers invite the dragon to share a picnic of fruit, beans and vegetables. After the picnic, the dragon feels strong for the first time, and he gives the town its energy back.

Rehearsal began two weeks before the show. Every afternoon, the children practiced in the gym, and at every rehearsal something went wrong: a cape fell off, or a line was forgotten. At the final rehearsal, Leo, the boy who played Captain Pea, forgot his line completely. Instead of stopping, he decided to ad lib. "I am Captain Pea," he said, "and I am small, but I am full of protein!" Everyone laughed, and Ms. Abara told him he could ad lib that line in the real show, too.

The line became a gag that the whole class loved. Whenever a hero felt tired in the play, someone shouted, "Full of protein!" and the others jumped up again. By the night of the show, even the parents knew the gag.

On the night of the show, the gym was full. A local broadcaster had heard about the play and sent a camera team, and the next evening the broadcaster showed a short clip on the news. In the clip, the candy dragon sits on a blanket with the avengers, eating an apple, while Captain Pea explains that vegetables are "not a punishment, but a superpower."

After the show, the families held a real picnic on the school lawn. Ms. Abara noticed that several children filled their plates with vegetables without any reward. Nobody had to bribe them.

Questions:
Why did Ms. Abara not want parents to bribe children with dessert?
She had read that when adults bribe children to eat a food, the children often decide that the food must be unpleasant.
How did Ms. Abara change the storyline?
Instead of slaying the dragon, the avengers invite him to share a picnic.
What happened at the final rehearsal?
Leo forgot his line, and he decided to ad lib.
What did the local broadcaster do?
It sent a camera team and showed a short clip on the evening news.
What did the children do at the real picnic?
Several children filled their plates with vegetables without any reward.

lessons.title: Harvest Festival
lessons.summary: How churches in Britain celebrate the harvest, and how a retired lawyer in a Scottish town turned the old custom into help for local families.
lessons.text:
In the United States, the great food holiday of the fall is Thanksgiving, celebrated at home around a turkey. In Britain, many people mark the end of the harvest in a different way: with a harvest festival, held in a church in late September or early October.

In 1843, a priest named Robert Hawker invited the farmers of his parish in Cornwall to a special service to give thanks for the harvest. The idea spread quickly, and within a few decades harvest festivals were held across the country. Today they are celebrated everywhere from tiny village churches to great cathedrals, where the service may be led by a bishop or even an archbishop. When an archbishop leads it, the gifts of food are the same as in any village: apples, potatoes, bread and jars of jam.

In England, the gifts are traditionally heaped around the altar, the table at the front of the church. People decorate the walls and windows with wheat, flowers and dark green ivy, and the smell of apples fills the building. Children often carry baskets of food up to the altar during the service.

In Scotland, where many people still call a church a kirk, the festival looks much the same, but the words are slightly different. The national church of Scotland traditionally does not speak of an altar; it uses the plain term "communion table." Yet a harvest morning in a stone kirk, its walls covered in ivy and its tables full of fruit, feels familiar to any visitor from England.

In the past, the food was shared among the poor of the parish. Today, it usually goes to a local food bank, and in one small Scottish town, this change was the work of a retired solicitor named Margaret Fraser. In Britain, a solicitor is a lawyer who advises people on matters such as wills, houses and family business. For thirty years, Margaret had worked as a solicitor in the town, and she knew which families were struggling. After she retired, she offered to organize the harvest collection.

Under her care, the collection grew from a few baskets to a full truck. She asked people to bring canned fish, rice, beans and other foods that keep for months, along with fresh apples from their gardens. Volunteers sorted everything in the church hall, and the food bank received enough to last until spring.

Last year, the town council made Margaret a freeman of the town, an old honor given to people who have served their community for many years. Being a freeman brings no money and no power; in the past, it gave certain rights to trade, but today it is simply a way of saying thank you. At the ceremony, Margaret said that the honor belonged to every family who had carried a basket to the kirk.

Questions:
When are harvest festivals usually held in Britain?
They are usually held in late September or early October.
Who started the modern harvest festival, and where?
A priest named Robert Hawker started it in his parish in Cornwall in 1843.
Where are the gifts placed in an English church?
They are traditionally heaped around the altar, the table at the front of the church.
What is a kirk?
It is a Scottish word for a church.
Why did the town council make Margaret a freeman of the town?
She had served her community for many years, and she had organized the harvest collection for the food bank.
